evidence: Ter. And. 3.3.23: amantium īrae amōris integrātiōst (Lewis & Short, s.v. amō)
Verg. A. 4.296: quis fallere possit amantem? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The participle of amāre as a noun: one who is in love, man or woman. Cicero sets it against amātor: aliud est amātōrem esse, aliud amantem (Tusc. 4.27).

evidence: Cic. Att. 1.20: vir bonus amātorque noster (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In a good sense a friend, an admirer, a lover of something: rūris, pācis, antīquitātis. Of love between people it is often the gallant or the paramour of comedy; the feminine is amātrīx.

terms.latin: amīca, amīcae f.; amīcus, amīcī m.
evidence: Catull. 72.3: dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam
terms.comment: Properly a friend; amīca is also a man’s girl, and in comedy often a mistress or courtesan (Lewis & Short), so it needs a context that makes the sense plain.

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.244: dē amīculā rīxātus (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam, sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs
phrases.english: I loved you then not just as the common man loves his girl, but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law

phrases.latin: ego illum audīvī in amōrem haerēre apud nesciō quam fidicinam
phrases.english: I heard he was stuck on some lyre-girl or other

sources: Lewis & Short: amo · Lewis & Short: amator · Lewis & Short: amicus · Lewis & Short: amatrix
Catullus from the Latinitas loci collection (loci-catullus); the other passages as Lewis & Short quotes them.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
